Summary

This work gathers and analyses quantitative morphological data of the development of Drosophila sensory neurons during larval development. The manuscript documents growth and retraction of neurites, giving an overall picture of how dendrites on a specific class of proprioceptors develop and how the developmental process may optimise the shape of the dendritic tree to sense bending. The authors propose a parsimonious stochastic optimization model for how neurites might grow, subject to constraints such as wiring cost. This model is found to give a good account of the data.

The reviewers raised several points that the authors should address in a revision of the paper. These are summarised here; the full reviewer comments are included below for reference and need not be addressed point-by-point. The reviewers agreed that no further experiments are necessary.

1) Check/provide evidence that the sampling rate of the time lapse imaging doesn't alias the measurements of dendritic growth and/or present a problem for relating data to the model.

2) Small variations in the model were identified – how are these justified (Figure 6B vs 2D)?

3) The authors should consider balancing their citations toward invertebrate quantitative neuroanatomy and existing quantitative/computational development studies.

4) Additional data for Figure 5A (as a figure supplement) would aid intuition.

Reviewer #1:

This study gathers and analyses quantitative morphological data of the development of Drosophila sensory neurons during larval development. They document growth and retraction of neurites in a very accessible and comprehensive way, giving a nice overall picture of how dendrites on a specific class of proprioceptors develop. The authors propose a parsimonious stochastic optimization model for how neurites might grow, subject to constraints such as wiring cost. This model is found to give a good account of the data.

The manuscript is well presented and methodologically sound. The conclusions are justified. The study should be of broad interest to developmental anatomists, theoretical biologists, neurophysiologists and the connectomics community.

It could be published as-is but would possibly benefit from more balanced and carefully curated scholarship: a lot of the citations in the Introduction concern mouse/rat neurophysiology, neglecting a lot of invertebrate studies. It is nice to connect the findings to dendritic function, but I feel the emphasis on dendritic physiology (e.g. computation in the visual system) is not balanced fairly against the (huge) amount of recent quantitative neuroanatomy work done in this very organism. Similarly, there is an omission of a lot of quantitative developmental work (both modelling and experiment, going back decades). Finally, there are a number of tangential studies that seem to be cited just to bulk up the references. I think the paper will be better received and will benefit the field more if the references could be rebalanced a little, should the authors wish to do so.

Reviewer #2:

The complexity of dendrite development has so far made it difficult to quantitatively describe their growth accurately. This work features in vivo imaging of a Drosophila sensory neuron called vpda, together with a convincing computational model that accurately describes most features of its development. In this aspect, the work is very interesting and poses a significant advance in regard to the quantitative description and understanding of dendritic tree growth and refinement during development. It further considers the functional aspects of vpda, based on curvature analysis and optimization of dendrite orientation for its proprioceptive function. Overall, I believe this is very interesting and thorough work shedding new insight into the little understood rules of dendritic tree development.

1) The embryonic imaging of vpda neurons was performed at 5min intervals, but quantifications were done only at 0.5-1h intervals. This might severely underestimate the growth dynamics during this stage, as dendrites can grow several microns within few minutes. Yet most of the authors' assumptions are based on this analysis. I think in particular growth and retraction rates might be potentially misrepresented, as both can happen to the same branch during the analyzed 30-60 min time intervals. The authors should at least consider this point and make a statement in this regard, or ideally validate their assumptions by analyzing their data at higher temporal resolution.

2) A very complementary preprint (Palavalli et al., 2020) describing and modelling vpda growth arrives at a similar conclusion as the work presented here. However, the computational models differ. Unlike here, the other model considers contact based self-repulsion (mediated by Dscam) as a key feature, resulting in similar simulated dendrite morphologies. I feel it is intriguing that both models basically arrive at the same result, yet the underlying assumptions differ. In my mind, this suggests that different growth mechanisms can result in similar outcomes. Alternatively, self-avoidance is not the only mechanism contributing to 2nd order branch parallelization, but acts in concert with stochastic retraction as described here. As dendrite self-avoidance is nonetheless a major feature of dendrite development from a biological point of view, likely across species and most neurons, the authors should discuss this point more carefully. Can they speculate about a biological correlate for the assumptions they make in their model, which results in stochastic retraction? As most of the parameters of the authors' model are directly derived from experimental data, this might inadvertently include the requirements for self-avoidance.

3) The authors show a very interesting computational analysis of dendrite curvature during larval locomotion, which coincides with neuronal calcium responses. While this result is not entirely novel as stated by the authors (see Vaadia et al., 2019), it still implies that dendrite development is adjusted to optimize its purpose. It is intriguing that the retraction of dorsoventral vpda dendrites coincides with peristaltic activity of the developing animal during the late embryonic stage. For the motor system, a critical period has been postulated around 17-19 h AEL, where rhythmic peristalsis and coordinated activity of motor neurons emerges. Have the authors considered a role for activity in reshaping of the dendritic tree during this phase, particularly during the retraction phase? It would be fairly straight forward to test this by Kir2.1-mediated silencing of vpda, providing a biological correlate shaping the final dendritic morphology.

Reviewer #3:

In the submitted manuscript, Castro and colleagues investigate the development of the dendritic tree of the c1vpda neurons of the Drosophila, by using a combination of in vivo imaging techniques and modelling of synthetic morphologies. The main conclusion of this study is that, during embryonic development, dendritic growth follows the optimal wire principle and that the subsequent stochastic retraction of dendritic branches allows for the maturation of a functional dendritic tree. Overall, the paper describes in detail this developmental process and is of potential wider interest as it showcases how stochastic processes can result in specialized dendritic tree patterns. I also appreciate the authors making their data and code available for the review process. I support this work for publication in eLife, yet I have some comments that would increase the clarity and visibility of the author's results.

1) My main concern has to do with the computational model shown in Figure 6, in combination with the model in Figure 2D/Figure 6B, dashed line. Specifically, I found it confusing why the authors chose to implement two different approaches to model dendritic growth. The results presented Figure 6B seem to better model the experimental data of Figure 2D, for a low number of branch points. The main differences between the two models, as far as I can tell, are in the surface area used to position the random targets and the inclusion of distinct time points. In other words, how are the two approaches different, and do they convey a principle for the developmental growth of the dendrites?

2) The results shown in Figure 5A are interesting and support the author's claim for the random retraction of dendrites. Can the authors provide information regarding the properties of the terminal branches (distributions of length, angle and BLO) that will make these results more intuitive?

results.result: Long-term time-lapse imaging reveals a sequence of c1vpda dendrite differentiation stages from embryonic to larval development, including main branch polarization, lateral branch extension with cycles of growth and retraction, a retraction phase, stabilization, and post-embryonic isometric scaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C30-C42 collectively describe the developmental trajectory observed through time-lapse imaging (Figure 1). The sequence of stages is directly observed in the imaging data, with clear morphological changes documented at specific time points. The isometric scaling in larval stages is supported by both imaging data and citation to prior work (Parrish et al., 2009).

results.result: tSNE analysis of 49 morphometric features shows that developmental time is a strong source of morphological variation, with early embryonic stages showing non-linear trajectories reflecting intense dynamics, and later larval stages showing more linear trajectories corresponding to isometric stretching.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 describe the tSNE analysis shown in Figure 2A. The visualization clearly shows temporal clustering and the described trajectory patterns. The interpretation linking non-linear trajectories to dynamic outgrowth/refinement and linear trajectories to isometric stretching is consistent with the imaging data in Figure 1.

results.result: Throughout development, c1vpda dendrites respect minimum wire constraints, as demonstrated by square root scaling relationships between dendrite length, surface area, and number of branch points that match predictions from optimal wire theory and synthetic MST-based models.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C62-C63 describe the wire optimization analysis in Figure 2D. The square root scaling relationships are clearly demonstrated in the data, and the fit to synthetic MST models (R²=0.98) provides strong quantitative support. This is a key finding linking developmental morphology to optimization principles.

results.result: The embryonic retraction phase preferentially eliminates shorter, proximally located, higher-order lateral branches (64.9% reduction) while largely preserving second-order lateral branches (19.1% reduction), reshaping the overall branch angle distribution toward higher angles along the anteroposterior axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54, C64, C67-C70 describe the selective effects of retraction shown in Figure 3. The quantitative measurements of branch reduction by order, median branch lengths and angles before and after retraction, and the shift in angle distributions are all directly supported by the data. The inference about proximal location is consistent with the morphological observations.

results.result: c1vpda neurons respond to body wall contraction with prominent dendritic Ca2+ signals, and modeling shows that branch curvature increases with orientation angle, such that branches oriented along the anteroposterior axis experience maximal curvature during contraction. Retraction preferentially removes low-curvature branches, suggesting functional constraints shape dendrite patterning.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79, C83-C84 integrate functional imaging (Figure 4A) with geometric modeling (Figure 4B) and morphological analysis (Figure 4D). The Ca2+ imaging replicates prior findings (Vaadia et al., 2019), the curvature modeling is mathematically sound, and the selective retraction of low-curvature branches is quantitatively demonstrated. The inference about functional constraints is well-supported by the convergent evidence.

results.result: In silico simulations comparing different retraction schemes (short branches first, low angles first, high branch order first, random) show that only random retraction yields good results across all morphometrics. Branch tracking analysis confirms retraction is stochastic in nature, yet this stochasticity supports optimal mechanical responsiveness.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86, C97-C98 describe the retraction simulations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and branch tracking analysis (Figure 5B). The comparison of retraction schemes is systematic and the conclusion that random retraction best fits the data is clearly supported. The finding that stochastic retraction can produce functionally optimized morphologies is a key conceptual result.

results.result: Branch tracking reveals that extension and reduction rates are similar and time-invariant across branch types (~2-3 μm/hr), but the proportion of branches in different states varies over time, with an initial phase of intense dynamics (~50% retracting) followed by a stabilization phase with decreased retraction and increased stable branches.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C96 describe the branch dynamics analysis shown in Figure 5B. The quantitative measurements of growth rates and the temporal changes in branch state proportions are directly supported by the tracking data. The inference of time-invariant mechanisms is reasonable given the consistent rates across the observation period.

results.result: A computational growth model combining stochastic growth satisfying wire constraints with random retraction accurately reproduces c1vpda morphogenesis, matching key morphometrics (branch points, total length, surface area), scaling relationships, branch length and angle distributions, and selective retraction of lower curvature branches.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C104 describe the computational model results shown in Figure 6. The model successfully reproduces multiple independent morphometric features (Figure 6C), scaling relationships (Figure 6B), and branch distributions (Figure 6D). The model is constrained by experimental data without parameter fitting, strengthening the conclusion that stochastic growth plus random retraction is consistent with the biological process.

results.result: The random retraction model slightly underestimates the orientation angle of second-order lateral branches after retraction (median model = 60.18° vs. real neurons = 63.93°), suggesting other mechanisms such as cell adhesion molecules may enhance growth direction preference.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 acknowledge a limitation of the model with specific quantitative comparison. The small discrepancy is honestly reported and the speculation about additional mechanisms (supported by citation to Hattori et al., 2013) is reasonable. This represents appropriate scientific caution about model limitations.

results.result: The study demonstrates that distinct sequential phases of stochastic growth and retraction achieve efficient dendritic trees optimized for both wire minimization and mechanical function, showing how dendrite growth balances structure-function requirements through self-organized developmental programs.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C29, C107-C108, C138, C156 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the experimental and modeling results. These conclusions are well-supported by the convergent evidence from time-lapse imaging, morphometric analysis, functional imaging, retraction simulations, and computational modeling presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: c1vpda proprioceptive neurons respond to body wall contractions during crawling, with dendritic branches oriented along the direction of contraction. Prior work has shown that c1da dendrite morphology is functionally important, with genetic or channel manipulations impairing crawling behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C16-C18, C20-C26 summarize established knowledge from prior work, supported by multiple citations. These claims provide essential background context for the study. The functional importance of c1da morphology is well-established in the literature cited.

results.result: The orientation of c1vpda branches along the direction of contraction may maximize membrane curvature during crawling, which could enhance mechanogated ion channel activation. Prior theoretical work on lipid bilayers shows curvature depends on membrane orientation, and recent work proposed c1da neurons are activated by membrane curvature increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C65, C72-C73, C147-C151 integrate prior theoretical and experimental work with the current study's modeling. The speculation about functional optimization is supported by the curvature modeling (Figure 4B) and is consistent with prior hypotheses (He et al., 2019; Vaadia et al., 2019). The proposal about second-order branches being better suited for mechanotransduction is a reasonable inference from the modeling.

results.result: c1vpda development begins with MB polarization in a consistent dorsal direction, followed by interstitial emergence of lateral branches. A combination of MB orientation, noisy filopodial exploration, and Dscam-based self-avoidance likely coordinates branch patterning, producing optimally wired, space-filling dendrites with distinct morphological classes of branches.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111, C114-C116 describe the early developmental process and propose mechanisms. The observations about MB polarization and lateral branch emergence are directly supported by Figure 1. The speculation about molecular mechanisms (C114) is reasonable given the extensive prior work cited, though not directly tested here. The wire optimization and space-filling properties are supported by Figure 2.

results.result: While prior low-resolution studies suggested sequential growth and retraction phases, higher-resolution studies showed concurrent dynamics. In c1vpda, parallel growth and retraction with changing proportions produces distinct phases. The biased retraction of higher-order branches results from asymmetric branch length distributions combined with random selection of branches for constant-amount retraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C124 contextualize the findings within prior literature and explain the mechanism of biased retraction. The observations of concurrent but proportionally changing dynamics are supported by Figures 1, 2, and 5. The mechanistic explanation (C122-C124) for how random retraction produces biased outcomes is a key insight well-supported by the data and simulations.

results.result: After retraction, c1vpda dendrites undergo stabilization and then isometric scaling during larval stages, preserving dendritic shape and complexity. This conservation suggests functional conservation during development, consistent with similar behavioral repertoires across larval stages. c1vpda neurons optimize both function and resources.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C137 describe the post-embryonic developmental phases supported by Figure 1B and the wire optimization analysis in Figure 2. The inference about functional conservation (C134) is reasonable given the morphological conservation. The citation to behavioral studies (C135) provides independent support. The conclusion about resource optimization (C136-C137) is supported by the wire minimization analysis.

results.result: The mechanism triggering stochastic retraction could be genetically determined, activity-dependent (potentially triggered by embryonic peristaltic waves), or competition-based (through intrinsic stabilization differences or contact-mediated retraction). Dscam-based machinery may implement programs equivalent to minimum spanning tree algorithms.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C131 present speculative hypotheses about mechanisms controlling retraction timing. While these are reasonable possibilities supported by citations to relevant prior work, they are explicitly speculative and not directly tested in this study. The Dscam hypothesis (C131) is particularly interesting given prior work by the authors, but remains speculative here.

results.result: Random retraction may be less costly to genetically encode than deterministic programs, representing an efficient self-organized mechanism for producing functionally specialized morphologies. Prior work shows multistage developmental programs incorporating stochasticity can generate stereotypical outcomes through molecular mechanisms utilizing stochasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88, C112-C113, C158-C159 discuss the conceptual implications of stochastic developmental mechanisms. While the specific claim about genetic encoding cost is speculative (C87, C159), the general principle is well-supported by the cited literature (Hiesinger and Hassan, 2018; Langen et al., 2015) and is consistent with the study's findings. This represents an important conceptual contribution.

results.result: Prior morphological models often rely on many parameters and provide phenomenological rather than mechanistic insights. Few have modeled development quantitatively or focused on retraction. The temporal resolution chosen here (1 hr intervals) was a trade-off between capturing dynamics and tracing speed, but the good model fit validates this choice.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C146 provide critical context about prior modeling work and justify methodological choices. The critique of prior models (C139-C142) is supported by citations. The justification for temporal resolution (C143) is honest about practical constraints. The validation through model fit (C144-C145) is supported by Figure 6. The forward-looking statement (C146) is reasonable.

results.result: c1da neurons have unique structural adaptations including denser microtubule arrays and firm anchoring to the epithelium, supporting their mechanosensory role. Similar adaptations are found in other mechanotransduction cells and in C. elegans, suggesting dendrite curvature may provide a conserved biophysical substrate for mechanosensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C155 synthesize structural observations from prior work (Delandre et al., 2016; Krieg et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2014; Albeg et al., 2011; Hall and Treinin, 2011) to support the functional interpretation. The inference about conserved mechanisms (C155) is reasonable given the cross-species evidence, though not directly tested here.

results.result: Similar developmental stages and strategies may be preserved across different cell types and species. Future work should elucidate mechanisms controlling temporal sequences of branch elaboration and determine the extent of similar self-organizing processes in other cell types, networks, and non-neuronal branching organs.
results.evaluation: Claims C157 and C160 discuss broader implications and future directions. The suggestion of conservation across cell types and species (C157) is supported by citations to comparative studies. results.result: Prior work has successfully linked dendrite geometry with ion channels for signal processing, and dendrite structure with wiring requirements for generating synthetic morphologies.
